cse-2005-cs-70.approach: In cycle-stealing mode the CPU loses exactly one memory cycle per transferred word, so the blocked fraction is (memory cycle time) / (time between successive words from the disk).

steps.title: Disk data rate
steps.body:
One track (512 sectors × 1 KB = 512 KB) passes the head per rotation; 3000 rpm = 50 rotations/s.

$$\text{rate} = 512 \times 1024 \times 50 = 26\,214\,400 \text{ B/s} \approx 26.2 \text{ MB/s}$$

steps.title: Time per 4-byte word
steps.body: $$t_{word} = \frac{4}{26\,214\,400} \text{ s} \approx 152.6 \text{ ns}$$

steps.title: Blocked fraction
steps.body:
Each word steals one 40 ns memory cycle:

$$\frac{40}{152.6} \approx 0.262 \approx 25\%$$

(With 1 KB = 1000 B: $4/25.6\text{ MB/s} = 156.25$ ns and $40/156.25 = 25.6\%$.) Closest option: **25**.

optionAnalysis.reason: 10% would need a word every 400 ns — about 2.6× slower than this disk.
Correct: 40 ns stolen out of every ≈ 152.6–156 ns ≈ 25–26%.
40% would need a word every 100 ns.
50% would need a word every 80 ns.

cse-2005-cs-70.shortcut: Fraction = cycle × (bytes/s ÷ word size) = 40 ns × 6.55 M words/s ≈ 0.26.
pitfalls: Surfaces and tracks per surface do not affect the rate — only one head transfers at a time.
Use bytes per rotation × rotations per second, not total capacity.
cse-2005-cs-70.verification: Words per second = 26 214 400 / 4 = 6 553 600; × 40 ns = 0.262 s of memory time per second ≈ 26%, i.e. option 25.

cse-2005-cs-71.approach: Worst case: every process holds $s_i - 1$ units and waits for one more. If even then one unit is left over, some process can finish, so deadlock is impossible: $\sum (s_i - 1) < m$.

steps.title: Worst-case deadlock state
steps.body: Deadlock needs every process blocked. A process with max need $s_i$ is blocked only while holding at most $s_i - 1$ units, so a deadlock can hold at most $\sum_{i=1}^{n}(s_i - 1)$ units with **all** $m$ units allocated.

steps.title: Sufficient condition
steps.body:
If $\sum_{i=1}^{n}(s_i - 1) < m$, at least one unit is always free when all processes wait, so some process can obtain its last unit, finish and release everything.

$$\sum_{i=1}^{n} s_i - n < m \iff \sum_{i=1}^{n} s_i < m + n$$

steps.title: Check the others
steps.body: $s_i < m$ for every $i$ (or $s_i < n$) does not stop $n$ processes from splitting all $m$ units and each waiting; $\sum s_i < mn$ is far weaker. Only (C) is sufficient.

optionAnalysis.reason: Counter-example: $m = 3$, $n = 3$, $s_i = 2$ satisfies $s_i < m$, yet each process can hold 1 unit (all 3 used) and wait for a second — deadlock.
Bounding each $s_i$ by $n$ says nothing about the total demand; $m = 2$, $n = 3$, $s_i = 2$: two processes hold one unit each and both wait — deadlock.
Correct: $\sum s_i < m + n$ means $\sum (s_i - 1) < m$, so a free unit always exists in the worst case.
$\sum s_i < mn$ allows e.g. $m = 3$, $n = 3$, $s_i = 2$ (sum 6 < 9), which can deadlock as shown for (A).

pitfalls: The reprint prints (b) the same as (a); the original (b) is $\forall i, s_i < n$.
cse-2005-cs-71.verification: Boundary: $m = 3$, $n = 3$, $s_i = 2$ gives $\sum s_i = 6 = m + n$ (condition fails) and indeed deadlocks; with $s_3 = 1$ the sum is 5 < 6 and $P_3$ always finishes, freeing a unit.

cse-2005-cs-72.approach: After fork the child gets a copy of the parent's address space: same virtual addresses, separate physical copies. The child adds 5, the parent subtracts 5.

steps.title: Values of a
steps.body: `fork()` returns 0 in the child, so the child prints $x = a + 5$ and the parent prints $u = a - 5$. Hence $u + 10 = x$.

steps.title: Addresses
steps.body: `&a` is a **virtual** address. The child is an identical copy of the parent's address space (copy-on-write only changes the physical frame), so the printed addresses are equal: $v = y$.

optionAnalysis.reason: $u = x + 10$ would mean the parent printed the larger value, but the parent subtracts 5.
Wrong sign relation and wrong address claim.
Correct: $x - u = (a+5) - (a-5) = 10$ and the virtual address of `a` is the same in both processes.
Value relation is right, but $v \ne y$ confuses physical with virtual addresses.

pitfalls: Copy-on-write gives different physical frames after the write, but programs only see virtual addresses.

cse-2005-cs-73.approach: With $h$ hops and $k$ packets of total size $p$, pipelining gives a delay proportional to $(k + h - 1)\,p$. Minimise over data sizes $d$ that divide 24.

steps.title: Delay model
steps.body:
Two intermediate nodes ⇒ $h = 3$ links. Packet size $p = d + 3$ (header 3 bytes), $k = 24/d$ packets. The first packet needs 3 transmission times, each later packet adds 1:

$$T \propto (k + 2)(d + 3)$$

steps.title: Optimum
steps.body: Minimum at $d = 6$ data bytes, i.e. packet size $p = 9$ bytes.

optionAnalysis.reason: Packet 4 (1 data byte): 26 × 4 = 104 byte-times — header overhead dominates.
Packet 6 (3 data bytes): 10 × 6 = 60.
Packet 7 (4 data bytes): 8 × 7 = 56.
Correct: packet 9 (6 data bytes): 6 × 9 = 54, the minimum.

pitfalls: Packet size in the options includes the 3-byte header.
cse-2005-cs-73.verification: Neighbouring sizes 8 (55) and 4 (56) are both worse than 6 (54).

cse-2005-cs-74.approach: For CSMA/CD the sender must still be transmitting when a collision indication returns: frame time ≥ RTT, plus the jamming signal that is sent on collision.

steps.title: Bits during one RTT
steps.body: $$46.4\ \mu\text{s} \times 10 \text{ Mbps} = 46.4 \times 10^{-6} \times 10^{7} = 464 \text{ bits}$$

steps.title: Add the jam
steps.body:
The 48-bit jam must also reach the sender while it is transmitting:

$$L_{min} = 464 + 48 = 512 \text{ bits}$$

optionAnalysis.reason: 94 has no basis (e.g. 46.4 + 48 mixes μs with bits).
416 = 464 − 48 subtracts the jam instead of adding it.
464 bits covers only the RTT and ignores the jam signal the question deliberately gives.
Correct: 464 + 48 = 512 bits (also the standard Ethernet 64-byte minimum).

pitfalls: The reprint prints "46.4 its" — it is μs.
Some sources give 464 by ignoring the jam; the jam is given for a reason.
cse-2005-cs-74.verification: 512 bits = 64 bytes, the IEEE 802.3 minimum frame size for 10 Mbps Ethernet (slot time 51.2 μs = 46.4 + 4.8 μs jam).

cse-2005-cs-75.approach: Each entity needs its own table; a 1:N relationship folds into the N-side table as a foreign key; an M:N relationship needs its own table.

steps.title: Entities
steps.body: $E_1$ and $E_2$ each need a table (simple single-valued attributes, no extra tables for attributes): 2 tables.

steps.title: Relationships
steps.body:
$R_1$ (one-to-many) is represented by a foreign key in the "many"-side table — no new table. $R_2$ (many-to-many) needs a separate table with both keys.

$$2 + 0 + 1 = 3$$

Correct: $E_1$, $E_2$ (with $R_1$'s foreign key) and one table for $R_2$.
4 gives $R_1$ its own table, which is unnecessary for 1:N.

cse-2005-cs-77.approach: For each book B the subquery counts strictly more expensive books. B qualifies when fewer than 5 books cost more, i.e. B is among the top 5 by price.

steps.title: Rank by count
steps.body: With distinct prices, the most expensive book has 0 costlier books, the 2nd has 1, …, the $k$-th has $k - 1$.

steps.title: Apply < 5
steps.body: $k - 1 < 5 \iff k \le 5$, so the query returns the titles of the five most expensive books.

The comparison `T.price > B.price` counts costlier books, so it ranks from the expensive end, and returns several rows, not one.
One title only would need `= 4`.

cse-2005-cs-78.approach: Attributes that never appear on a right-hand side (E, H) must be in every key; then add the fewest attributes needed to reach all of R.

steps.title: Mandatory attributes
steps.body: RHS attributes are B, D, C, A. E and H never appear on a right side, so every key contains EH. $(EH)^+ = \{E, H, C\}$ — not a key.

steps.title: Minimality
steps.body: Each is minimal because $EH$ alone is not a key. So the candidate keys are AEH, BEH, DEH.

optionAnalysis.reason: AE and BE miss H, which no FD derives.
Same problem: none contains H.
BCH lacks E, and $(BCH)^+ = \{A,B,C,D,H\}$ never gets E.
Correct: the three closures above cover R and EH alone does not.

cse-2005-cs-79.approach: On a single bus only one register can drive the bus per cycle, and the ALU reads only from S and T. So the two operands go to S and T in separate cycles and the sum returns over the bus in a third.

steps.title: Cycle 1
steps.body: $S \leftarrow R0$ (R0 drives the bus).

steps.title: Cycle 2
steps.body: $T \leftarrow R1$ (R1 drives the bus; it cannot share cycle 1, since the bus carries one value).

steps.title: Cycle 3
steps.body:
$R0 \leftarrow S + T$ (ALU output drives the bus back into the GPR file).

Minimum = **3** cycles.

optionAnalysis.reason: 2 would need both operands on the single bus in the same cycle.
Correct: S←R0, T←R1, R0←S+T.
4 adds an unneeded extra transfer; the ALU output feeds the bus directly.
5 counts memory cycles, but add R0,R1 never touches memory during execution.

pitfalls: The execution cycle excludes instruction fetch.
cse-2005-cs-79.verification: Bus usage: R0, R1, ALU-out — three distinct values, one per cycle, so 3 is a lower bound and achievable.

cse-2005-cs-80.approach: PC already points to the second word (the address `sub`). One bus cycle can copy PC into both MAR and S; the memory read and the ALU increment then overlap, and PC is loaded from MDR last.

steps.title: Cycle 1
steps.body: PC drives the bus: $MAR \leftarrow PC$ and $S \leftarrow PC$ in the same cycle (one value, two destinations).

steps.title: Cycle 2
steps.body: Memory loads $MDR \leftarrow M[MAR]$ over the **memory** bus, while the ALU computes $S + 1$ and drives the internal bus: $Rn \leftarrow PC + 1$.

steps.title: Cycle 3
steps.body:
$PC \leftarrow MDR$ (MDR drives the bus).

Minimum = **3** cycles.

optionAnalysis.reason: 2 is impossible: the memory read alone needs the MAR-load cycle plus the MDR-load cycle, and PC ← MDR needs one more bus cycle.
Correct with maximal overlap: {MAR, S ← PC}, {MDR ← M, Rn ← S+1}, {PC ← MDR}.
4 results if the increment is not overlapped with the memory read.
5 results if every micro-operation gets its own cycle (no overlap at all).

pitfalls: The question asks for the **minimum**, so allowed overlaps must be used.
The answer is debated (3 vs 4/5) because it depends on whether the internal bus can carry the ALU result while MDR is filled from the memory bus.
cse-2005-cs-80.verification: Dependencies: PC ← MDR needs the read (2 cycles) to finish first, so 3 is a lower bound; the schedule above achieves it.

cse-2005-cs-81a.approach: Space of a recursive function = maximum depth of the call stack × space per frame. Time is exponential, but only one chain of calls is live at any moment.

steps.title: Deepest chain
steps.body: foo(n) calls foo(n−1) (among others), which calls foo(n−2), … down to foo(0): depth $n + 1$.

steps.title: Space
steps.body:
Each frame stores `n`, `i`, `sum` — $O(1)$. Calls in the loop run one after another, so frames are reused.

$$S(n) = O(n)$$

optionAnalysis.reason: Ignores the recursion stack, which grows to depth $n$.
Correct: Recursion depth for foo(n) is n (foo(n) → foo(n−1) → … → foo(0)), each frame O(1).
$O(n!)$ confuses space with a (wrong) bound on the number of calls.
$O(n^n)$ has no basis; the number of calls is $2^{n}$ anyway, and calls are not simultaneous.

pitfalls: Time is $\Theta(2^n)$ (foo(n) makes $2^n$ calls in total), but space only counts frames that are live at the same time.
cse-2005-cs-81a.verification: foo(3): live stack at its deepest is foo(3)→foo(2)→foo(1)→foo(0) = 4 frames = n + 1.

cse-2005-cs-81b.approach: Memoisation stores foo(0)…foo(n−1) in a table of n entries; the recursion depth is still at most n. Both are O(n).

steps.title: Table
steps.body: Values foo(i), $0 \le i < n$, are stored: $n$ doubles → $O(n)$.

steps.title: Stack
steps.body: The recursion still goes at most $n$ deep → $O(n)$. Total $O(n) + O(n) = O(n)$. (Time drops from exponential to $O(n^2)$, or $O(n)$ with a running sum.)

optionAnalysis.reason: A table of $n$ stored values cannot be $O(1)$.
Correct: $n$ table entries plus at most $n$ stack frames.
$O(n^2)$ is the modified **time** (n calls × loop of up to n), not space.
$O(n!)$ is unrelated to the n stored values.

cse-2005-cs-81b.verification: Only distinct arguments 0…n−1 are ever stored, one double each.

cse-2005-cs-82a.approach: Cut property: with distinct weights, the lightest edge crossing any cut belongs to the (unique) minimum spanning tree.

steps.title: Cut property
steps.body: [X, Y] is a cut and $e$ is its unique minimum crossing edge. If an MST $T$ omitted $e$, adding $e$ makes a cycle that crosses the cut again through another edge $f$ with $w(f) > w(e)$; swapping $f$ for $e$ gives a lighter spanning tree — contradiction.

steps.title: Other options fail
steps.body: Shortest and longest s–t paths, or every s–t path, need not use $e$ — e.g. a direct heavy-but-short route s–t may beat a route through $e$.

answer.value: The minimum weighted spanning tree of G

optionAnalysis.reason: Correct: cut property (unique because weights are distinct).
Counter-example: $s$–$t$ edge of weight 3, and $e$ = $s$–$u$ of weight 1 with $u \in Y$, $u$–$t$ weight 10: shortest path is the direct edge 3 and avoids $e$.
Any other crossing edge gives an s–t path avoiding $e$ (e.g. the direct $s$–$t$ edge above).
The longest path can also avoid $e$; nothing ties maximal paths to the lightest crossing edge.

pitfalls: The reprint has a blank (a) and lists the four real options as (b)–(e); here they are relabelled A–D as in the original paper.
cse-2005-cs-82a.verification: Kruskal processes edges in increasing order; $e$ is the first edge joining a component in X with one in Y, so it never closes a cycle and is always accepted.

cse-2005-cs-82b.approach: Minimum spanning trees are also minimum bottleneck (minimax) trees: the unique s–t path in the MST minimises the maximum edge weight among all s–t paths.

steps.title: Suppose a better path exists
steps.body: Let $P$ be the s–t path in the MST with heaviest edge $f$, and $Q$ an s–t path whose every edge is lighter than $f$.

steps.title: Contradiction
steps.body: Removing $f$ splits the MST into two parts with $s$, $t$ on opposite sides; $Q$ must cross this cut with some edge $g$, $w(g) < w(f)$. Replacing $f$ by $g$ gives a lighter spanning tree — contradiction. So the MST path has minimum congestion.

answer.value: A path from s to t in the minimum weight spanning tree

optionAnalysis.reason: Correct: MST paths are minimax paths (proof by cut exchange).
Shortest path minimises the **sum**: e.g. direct s–t edge of weight 10 versus s–u–t with weights 6 and 6 — sum 10 < 12 but congestion 10 > 6.
An Euler walk uses every edge, so its congestion is the maximum edge weight of the graph.
A Hamiltonian path visits every vertex and may be forced through heavy edges; it may not even exist.

cse-2005-cs-82b.verification: In the example of (B), the MST takes 6 and 6 (not 10), so its s–t path has congestion 6 — the true minimum.

cse-2005-cs-83a.approach: The grammar is ambiguous, so the LALR(1) table has shift-reduce conflicts on + and ×; yacc reports them and, by default, resolves each in favour of shift.

steps.title: Where the conflict arises
steps.body: After reading $E + E$ with lookahead + or ×, the parser can reduce by $E \to E + E$ or shift the operator — a shift-reduce conflict (same for $E × E$). No two productions share a right-hand side, so there is no reduce-reduce conflict.

steps.title: yacc default
steps.body: Without `%left`/`%right`/precedence declarations, yacc reports the S/R conflicts and resolves each in favour of **shift**.

answer.value: Shift-reduce conflict, resolved in favour of shift

optionAnalysis.reason: yacc never eliminates recursion; LR parsers handle left recursion directly.
There is no reduce-reduce conflict (yacc would pick the earlier production in that case).
Correct: default resolution of an S/R conflict is shift.
Reduce is yacc's default only for reduce-reduce conflicts (earlier rule), not shift-reduce.

cse-2005-cs-83a.verification: Running yacc/bison on this grammar reports "4 shift/reduce conflicts" and the y.output file shows them resolved as shift.

cse-2005-cs-83b.approach: Always shifting means the parser keeps reading operators before reducing, so the rightmost operator is applied first: both operators get equal precedence and right associativity.

steps.title: Parse 3 × 2 + 1
steps.body: Stack $E × E$ with lookahead +: conflict → shift +. Then reduce $E + E$ (2 + 1 = 3) first, then $E × E$ (3 × 3).

steps.title: Value
steps.body:
$$3 \times (2 + 1) = 9$$
Similarly $a + b × c$ would give $a + (b × c)$: operators group to the right regardless of kind — equal precedence, right associative.

optionAnalysis.reason: Left associativity would need reduce-before-shift; that gives (3 × 2) + 1 = 7.
Correct: always shift ⇒ right grouping ⇒ 3 × (2 + 1) = 9.
That is the usual arithmetic convention, achievable only with precedence declarations.
+ above × with left associativity is not what default shift produces.
